questions.questionText: How does spear phishing differ from generic mass phishing?

options.text: Spear phishing is automated using pop-up advertisements
Spear phishing is highly targeted at a specific individual or team using researched details
Spear phishing only targets mobile phones using text messages
Spear phishing requires physical entry into an office building

questions.explanation: Spear phishing relies on prior reconnaissance to tailor realistic messages directly to specific targets.

questions.questionText: Public professional profiles on LinkedIn can provide attackers with information used to craft spear phishing messages.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: True. Attackers mine job titles, reporting structures, vendor software, and current projects from LinkedIn profiles to build convincing pretexts.

questions.questionText: A vendor you've never worked with emails you a password-protected .zip file labeled "Invoice_Overdue.zip" and asks you to enter the password from a separate message to open it. Why might an attacker package a malicious attachment this way?

options.text: To save hard drive storage space on remote laptops
To prevent email security gateways from scanning the encrypted contents for malware
To make the file download faster over home Wi-Fi networks
Because password protection automatically executes scripts

questions.explanation: Email gateway scanners cannot inspect encrypted archive contents without the password, allowing malicious payloads past boundary defenses.

questions.questionText: Which public sources are commonly harvested by adversaries during the OSINT phase of a spear phishing campaign? (Select ALL that apply)

options.text: LinkedIn corporate organizational charts
Public GitHub code repositories detailing software libraries
Personal social media posts detailing travel or conference attendance
Encrypted database servers operating behind private firewalls

questions.explanation: LinkedIn, GitHub, and social media posts provide open public data. Private encrypted database servers are not public OSINT sources.

questions.questionText: Spear phishing can target remote staff based on their system access, administrative privileges, financial responsibilities, or public profile; it is not limited to executives.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: The lesson identifies remote staff with system access, administrative privileges, financial responsibilities, or public profiles as its audience.

questions.questionText: Public details on LinkedIn, GitHub, or social media can be combined to personalize a spear-phishing lure.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: The lesson explains that attackers combine publicly available profile, project, and social-media details to make a lure more personal.

questions.questionText: An email claiming to be from your company's HR department contains a link to “Updated W-2 Tax Forms.” The link URL points to an external domain unrelated to your company. What is the safest course of action?

options.text: Follow the link after checking that the message mentions HR.
Do not click; verify the request with HR through a known work contact or official channel, then report it.
Reply and ask the sender to confirm your employee ID before using the link.
Forward the link to a coworker and ask them to test it.

questions.explanation: The lesson recommends verifying unusual requests independently through a trusted contact method rather than relying on a message link.

questions.questionText: Spear phishing relies solely on technical software exploits and does not use psychological manipulation.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Spear phishing is a socio-technical attack combining technical delivery vectors with psychological manipulation (trust, urgency, authority).

questions.questionText: What should you do before opening an unexpected password-protected archive from an external party?

options.text: Open it on a personal device because the archive came from an external party.
Confirm the request through a trusted contact method before opening or extracting the archive.
Ask the sender for the password in the same message thread, then extract the files.
Extract a copy of the archive before verifying who sent it.

questions.explanation: The lesson warns that password-protected archives may be difficult for scanners to inspect and says to confirm unexpected requests before opening attachments.

questions.questionText: An attacker researching you before sending a spear-phishing email finds your public GitHub profile. What information could they gather there to make their message more believable?

options.text: Your private home Wi-Fi password
Public projects, repositories, programming frameworks, and technologies
Your hardware MFA seed keys
Your credit card PIN

questions.explanation: The lesson's GitHub example covers public projects, repositories, programming frameworks, and technologies.

questions.questionText: What does the acronym "OSINT" stand for in cybersecurity reconnaissance?

options.text: Operational System Internal Network Tracking
Open Source Intelligence
Optical Security Inspection for Network Traffic
Offline Storage Integration and Networking Tool

questions.explanation: OSINT stands for Open Source Intelligence, referring to publicly available data mined from social platforms, repositories, and directories.

questions.questionText: Enabling macros on an unverified Microsoft Word or Excel attachment is safe as long as the document has a .docm extension.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: False. The .docm extension explicitly denotes a macro-enabled document. Enabling macros runs underlying VBA code that can install malware.

questions.questionText: You are a remote graphic designer. You receive a direct message on Telegram from someone claiming to be a senior manager at your main client account, asking you to open Design_Brief.pdf.exe. How should you react?

options.text: Open the file immediately since it contains "pdf" in the filename
Do not open the file; the double extension (.pdf.exe) indicates an executable file
Rename the file to .doc and then double-click it
Forward the file to a friend on personal social media

questions.explanation: Files ending in .exe are executable programs. The .pdf.exe naming convention tricks users into opening executable malware.

questions.questionText: A message that mentions a real project or travel detail is safe to trust because the detail is accurate.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Public information can make a spear-phishing lure convincing. The lesson advises verifying unusual requests using a trusted contact method.

questions.questionText: Which practices match the attachment-safety guidance taught in this lesson? (Select ALL that apply)

options.text: Check the full filename and watch for a double extension such as report.pdf.exe
Enable unexpected macros so you can inspect the document content
Run an unexpected attachment with administrator privileges to see what it contains
Do not enable unexpected macros, and verify an unexpected file transfer with the sender through a trusted channel

questions.explanation: The lesson warns about disguised double extensions and unexpected macros and recommends confirming unexpected files through a trusted channel.

questions.questionText: A spear phisher notices on Twitter that your company’s Lead Developer is on a 14-hour flight. The attacker emails you posing as the Lead Developer, requesting emergency production database credentials. Should you comply?

options.text: True (Comply immediately)
False (Do not comply)

questions.explanation: False. Attackers exploit travel schedules to create situations where the spoofed identity cannot be reached easily. Always follow established verification protocols.

questions.questionText: An unexpected attachment asks you to enable macros before you can read it. What should you do?

options.text: Enable the macros because the document says they are required
Do not enable them; verify the request with the sender through a trusted contact method
Forward the file to a personal account and open it there
Rename the attachment and open it without checking with the sender

questions.explanation: The lesson says not to enable unexpected macros and to confirm an unexpected attachment with the sender before opening it.

questions.questionText: Which attachment clues match risks taught in this lesson? (Select TWO)

options.text: The filename ends in .pdf.exe, making an executable look like a PDF
An .xlsm document asks you to enable macros before viewing its contents
The file is a plain PDF and does not ask you to take an unexpected action
The sender is verified and the file is confirmed through an approved company channel

questions.explanation: The lesson specifically warns about disguised double extensions and unexpected macro-enabled Office files.

questions.questionText: A freelancer receives an unexpected file named Project_Brief.pdf.exe and is urged to open it immediately. What makes this attachment suspicious?

options.text: The familiar project wording proves it came from an approved client folder
The final .exe extension indicates it is an executable, so do not open it before verifying the request
The file is suspicious only because it is being sent to a freelancer
Changing its filename would remove the executable content

questions.explanation: The lesson uses names such as report.pdf.exe to show how a double extension can disguise an executable as a document.

questions.questionText: An email claims to be from HR, but its sender address uses an unrelated external domain. What should you do?

options.text: Trust the message because its display name matches the HR department
Do not follow the link; verify the request through a known HR contact or official work channel
Reply to the message and ask the sender to repeat your employee details
Open the link in a private browser window before deciding whether it is genuine

questions.explanation: The lesson teaches independent verification of unusual requests and warns that a message's apparent identity does not make its request trustworthy.
